acts.act_one: Opens with a 1976 prologue in Venice establishing the foundational paternal vow ('I never had a dad. That's not going to happen to him'), then jumps five years to 1981 San Francisco to introduce the socioeconomic trap: thirty unsellable bone density scanners, mounting parking tickets, a decaying marriage, and a cheap daycare with 'Happyness' misspelled on the wall. The inciting incident occurs when Chris encounters a Ferrari-driving stockbroker and learns the profession requires mathematical aptitude rather than a college degree. Act One escalates through a relentless chain of compounding physical and domestic obstacles—chasing a junkie who steals his scanner, solving a Rubik's Cube in a shared cab to win Jay Twistle's attention, fleeing a $17.30 cab fare, Linda walking out, and spending the night in jail for unpaid tickets—culminating in Chris showing up to the Dean Witter boardroom in paint-splattered clothes and accepting an unpaid six-month, 1-in-20 internship while retaining custody of his son.
acts.act_two: Structured as an economic and chronological vice ('This part of my life is called... intern') where upward professional mobility is pitted directly against downward domestic freefall. As Chris works the phones from the top down (targeting pension manager Walter Ribbon) and loses precious hours running humiliating errands for his manager Frakesh, his living situation systematically degrades: moving from the apartment to a residence motel, losing a scanner to a delusional street man ('Time Man') while getting hit by a car, and having his remaining bank balance wiped out by a $645.14 IRS garnishment. The midpoint pivots at the Candlestick Park corporate box: Chris fails to land Walter Ribbon's fund directly, but pivots to harvesting business cards from younger Bell Western executives. The low point strikes when Chris and Christopher are locked out of their motel and forced to spend the night on the floor of a locked transit station bathroom, with Chris pretending the broken scanner is a 'time machine' to shield his son from the trauma while silently weeping.
acts.act_three: Driven by a daily 5:00 PM ticking clock to secure a bed at the Almont Church shelter while carrying all their worldly possessions to the office and competing for the single broker slot. Chris hits physical and financial bottom—fighting in the shelter line, breaking his other thumb, giving his last five dollars to a Dean Witter partner for cab fare, and selling his blood to buy a Radio Shack Thompson wire. The climax is bifurcated into two quiet triumphs: first, repairing the last scanner by streetlight in the shelter ('This part of my life... is called happiness') to earn the $418 needed to survive the final weeks and sign thirty-one Bell Western accounts; second, being called into the partner boardroom on the final day ('Wear a shirt tomorrow... because tomorrow's going to be your first day'). Resolves with Chris holding back tears in the elevator, picking up Christopher under the 'Happyness' mural, and sitting on a bus bench intentionally letting a bus pass by without running after it.

mystery_hiding: Rather than concealing a narrative plot twist, the script operates on a mechanic of 'social concealment'—where the dramatic tension is built on how Chris hides his homelessness and poverty from the corporate world above him and the harsh reality of their destitution from the five-year-old beside him. To Dean Witter partners and Bell Western clients, luggage carried into the office is passed off as a 'work trip to Sacramento' or a 'golf outing', a lack of a car at Ribbon's house is masked by faking a sudden bee sting, and paint-covered clothes are disarmed with radical candor. To Christopher, a transit station restroom is reframed as a prehistoric 'cave' accessed via the scanner's 'time machine' button, and lack of electricity is framed as saving for breakfast. For the audience, the script maintains complete ledger transparency—explicitly showing every dwindling checkbook balance ($138.00, $64.08, $2.00) and decreasing scanner count via freeze-frame photography so the audience feels the exact mathematical impossibility of his survival before the final boardroom reveal.
character_connections: Anchored entirely by the symbiotic, protective tether between Chris and five-year-old Christopher, which serves as both Chris's ultimate handicap in the internship race (forcing him to leave work by 4:30 PM while childless peers work until 8:00 PM) and his sole emotional engine. Linda functions as an exhausted realist who breaks under the weight of Chris's deferred promises, exiting at the Act One break to raise the stakes to solo parenthood. Institutional authority figures are split between callous obstructors (Office Manager Alan Frakesh, who treats Chris as an errand boy and refuses to pay a parking ticket incurred moving his car; Mrs. Chu) and meritocratic gatekeepers (Jay Twistle and the First Partner, who respond to raw math ability, hustle, and humor). Finally, the delusional 'Time Man' (the Filipino man on the bus) acts as a surreal thematic foil—projecting fantasy onto Chris's hated scanner, which Chris later adopts to save his son's innocence in the station bathroom.
spine: A desperate father refuses to let systemic poverty break his vow to his son, enduring homelessness and grueling humiliation to cross the chasm from the bottom of the American underclass into financial security.
key_structural_decisions: Autobiographical chapter-labeling via voiceover ('This part's called Riding the Bus,' 'This part of my life's called... running,' 'Intern,' 'Happiness') that segments the narrative by physical state of endurance rather than conventional dates.

The Bone Density Scanner as a dual-purpose structural albatross and lifeline: physically weighing Chris down in every sprint across San Francisco, visually measuring his remaining time via freeze-frame montages of the shrinking stack in his living/motel room, and transforming at the low point from a hated financial mistake into a 'time machine' of fatherly imagination and the final $418 salvation.

Visible ledger and clock tyranny: cutting repeatedly to exact bank balances ($138.00, $64.08), exact prices ($418 commission, $480 bail, $645.14 IRS lien, $2 shelter beds), and towering wall clocks (2:42, 2:48, 2:55, 3:01, 3:17 during the missed Walter Ribbon appointment; 4:30 and 4:50 for the shelter line) to turn mundane poverty into a high-stakes thriller.

Kinetic motif of 'running' vs. 'sitting': structuring the entire middle of the script around frantic sprints after buses, trains, junkies, and appointments—only to resolve the film's thematic arc by having Chris and Christopher sit on a bench and deliberately watch a bus drive away without chasing it.

The 'bottom-to-top' inversion strategy: having Chris bypass the bottom of the cold-call sheet to call CEO/Pension Manager Walter Ribbon directly, which fails to land Ribbon's account at Candlestick Park but laterally yields the thirty-one junior executive accounts that win him the job.
scene_rhythm: A breathless, propulsive alternation between frantic, kinetic transit sequences (sprinting with forty-pound boxes, multi-transfer train/bus montages, ticking-clock errands) and quiet, claustrophobic domestic/nocturnal scenes with Christopher (washing up in shelter sinks, studying by streetlight, waiting on bus benches). Punctuated periodically by deadpan comedic micro-set-pieces (the Rubik's Cube cab ride, the dissolve-montage of the ignored parking ticket on Frakesh's leg, the fake bee sting) that relieve pressure just before the next financial blow lands.
